text: Ninety-nine point nine five percent uptime sounds like a complete answer, but it hides more than it reveals. It doesn't show whether that downtime was one clean incident or ten chaotic ones, it says nothing about latency that degraded without ever crossing into a full outage, and it says nothing about whether the team keeping that number healthy is sustainably staffed. A service can hit its uptime target every quarter while everything underneath it is quietly getting worse.

Mean time to resolution usually gets reported as one number, but it's really three different problems stacked together. MTTD is how long between the real problem starting and an alert actually firing — a high number there means a monitoring gap. MTTA is how long between the alert firing and a human acknowledging it — a high number there points at paging configuration or on-call fatigue. MTTR, counted from acknowledgment, is how long the real mitigation takes. Reporting only the combined total hides which of the three is the actual bottleneck, and each one needs a different fix.

Beyond MTTR, four more signals matter. Alert-to-noise ratio — actionable alerts divided by total alerts fired — predicts alert fatigue before it causes a missed page. On-call load distribution shows whether pages are spread fairly or concentrated on one person. Error budget burn rate shows how fast a service is spending its allowed unreliability. And postmortem action-item completion shows whether a team is actually closing the gaps incidents surface, or just writing them down and moving on.

On-call load specifically needs to be tracked per engineer, not just per team, because a reasonable team total can hide one person absorbing almost all the after-hours pages — usually because they're the only one who understands a particular subsystem. That's not just unfair, it's a single point of knowledge failure and a fast track to the burnout that Lesson 21 already connected to worse incident outcomes.

Read together — low detection time, a stable or improving alert-to-noise ratio, and evenly spread on-call load — these signals show whether a team running a service is actually in a sustainable, healthy state, which is what operational excellence really means. That same question of sustainability carries into the next chapter, where we look at building an SRE practice and culture that holds up as an organization grows.
